newsitem.title: GREECE: GREEK ECON MINISTER VOWS SUPER-TOUGH BUDGET.
newsitem.headline: GREEK ECON MINISTER VOWS SUPER-TOUGH BUDGET.

text.p: Greece is preparing the "toughest budget in 15 years" to ensure the country is ready for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) by the end of the century, National Economy and Finance Minister Yannos Papandoniou said.

"We hope by 1998 to be ready as regards the criteria in the Maastricht treaty - to have achieved inflation close to three percent and brought the debt to three percent of GDP," he said in an interview published in 'Ethnos' newspaper on Monday.
If the economy had not shaped up by 1998, Greece was in danger of becoming a "second-class" European Union partner.
"We risk losing EU funding...many of the projects under way will slide," Papandoniou said.

"Secondly and most importantly, we will lose the conditions of stability, which means low inflation, low interest rates which will grant us or strengthen our participation in a large group of industrialised nations, which have credibility and power," he said.
Failing to make the Maastricht grade would also mean losing Europe's support of Greece's national security, he added.

The budget for 1997 - which must be submitted to parliament this week - is calculated to get the wealthy and powerful to contribute to convergence, but "nobody can be totally excluded", the minister said.
Workers' demands that income brackets be readjusted for inflation cannot be satisfied, he said, in the interests of keeping inflation down.
"We could index income brackets if we imposed indirect taxes... We didn't because we believe that inflation is the worst enemy of real incomes," he said.
The same held for unionists' demands that the threshold for tax-free income be raised to two million drachmas, from the current one million.
"Such a change favours higher income earners rather than lower.. and the cost of such a change would be over 200 billion drachmas for the state budget. We didn't have those margins," he said.
Papandoniou said the government would not shy from chasing the affluent and that criticism of the budget by business and industry that it failed to adequately curtail public spending was misguided.
"The affluent and high income earners must realise that Greece is the country in which they pay less than any other European country," he said.

"Here, the affluent and high income earners manage to evade taxes in various ways not always illegally," he added. "At this time, for better or worse, there are significant margins not only to reduce the debt but to provide basic social justice. The affluent and high income earners will pay."

Tax evasion will be stamped on and loopholes in legislation will be closed, Papandoniou said. The finance ministry was working closely on these issues with the U.S. Internal Revenue Service (IRS) - a team is expected in Greece soon - and services in EU countries.
Papandoniou said Greece's economic woes were due to a lack of a stable and credible economic policy over the past two decades.

"But, of course, we are not so far behind as to believe we have missed the train. With work, I believe that at the turn of the century we will be in Europe. That is the aim of this government," he said. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
